Bowman, Modernizing Banking Supervision: A Shared Agenda for the Americas
items.excerpt: Speech At the ASBA-BCBS-FSI High-Level Meeting for the Americas on Banking Supervision, Brasília, Brazil (via pre-recorded video)
body: Accessible Keys for Video
[Space Bar] toggles play/pause;
[Right/Left Arrows] seeks the video forwards and back (5 sec );
[Up/Down Arrows] increase/decrease volume;
[M] toggles mute on/off;
[F] toggles fullscreen on/off (Except IE 11);
The [Tab] key may be used in combination with the [Enter/Return] key to navigate and activate control buttons, such as caption on/off.

Good morning.1 I would like to thank our hosts, the Banco Central do Brasil, the Association of Supervisors of Banks of the Americas (ASBA), the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS), and the Financial Stability Institute, for bringing us together. Banking supervisors around the world are tasked with ensuring the safety and soundness of the banking system. To be effective in this work, bank supervisory and regulatory frameworks must be forward looking to anticipate future risks. Today, I will discuss three ways in which modernizing our supervision and regulatory frameworks can enhance our ability to be effective.

First, we must learn the appropriate lessons from failures of supervisory effectiveness. Recent experience in the United States demonstrates that it is not sufficient to identify financial risks. Supervisors must also have the authority, accountability, and judgment to act before those risks are realized.

Second, our regulatory and supervisory frameworks must be regularly revisited to keep pace with the evolving financial landscape. These frameworks must focus on the most material risks, enable timely decisions, and adapt to rapidly changing financial markets and technologies. This is a priority both for the Federal Reserve and our international colleagues, including those on the Financial Stability Board (FSB) and the BCBS.

Third, banking supervisors throughout the Americas must be effective. Our shared history, deeply interconnected economies, and regional financial challenges support alignment of our interests in maintaining strong institutions for supervisory cooperation. ASBA can play a role in that effort.

These points are closely related. Effective supervision requires sound judgment. Sound judgment must be supported by modern frameworks. And cooperation among supervisors in the Americas supports strengthening both.

Learning from Banking Failures: Information Must Lead to Action One of the most valuable responsibilities of any supervisory authority is to learn the right lessons from failure and adjust accordingly.

The March 2023 failure of Silicon Valley Bank (SVB), and subsequent discussions about what went wrong and paths for reform, provide a useful case study. Extraordinary measures were taken to address banking system stress in the wake of SVB's failure, and fundamental questions remain regarding the effectiveness of the Federal Reserve System's supervisory function. Earlier reviews of the bank's failure provided important information but did not consider questions about shortcomings in the Federal Reserve's supervisory approach or identify opportunities to address long-standing weaknesses in our supervision. When I became Vice Chair for Supervision, I initiated an independent review of SVB's failure.
The initial findings of that review released in September were sobering. The review validated that supervisors identified the bank's fundamental vulnerabilities well before its failure.2

Those vulnerabilities included substantial interest rate risk, a highly concentrated and predominantly uninsured deposit base, and inadequate preparedness to meet liquidity demands. These were not unfamiliar or complicated risks to understand. They have been common risks throughout history, were present at the time of SVB's failure, and continue to be fundamental banking risks today. Yet our supervisory process failed to produce timely and effective action to address them.

A central lesson is that the failure of supervision was not a failure to obtain information. It was a failure to translate information into timely, decisive action. The review identified a long-standing supervisory problem of consultation without conclusion or action, uncertainty about decisionmaking authority, and a lack of accountability. Supervisors identified concerns, documented weaknesses, and discussed vulnerabilities. But the process did not result in prompt action to require the bank to address material risks that ultimately led to its failure.

One particularly revealing finding illustrates the problem. Between 2019 and March 2023, supervisors cited 54 supervisory matters that required attention. Yet no finding required SVB to shorten the maturity profile of its securities portfolio or restructure the held-to-maturity book, which were material financial risks that contributed to the bank's failure. Instead, many supervisory findings focused on process concerns. While interest rate risk was discussed, the approach criticized how the bank measured the risk but did not direct the bank to reduce it.

Supervisors engaged in extensive supervisory activity, produced considerable documentation, and created a substantial record of identified concerns. But the risks that were most material-the risks that affected the bank's financial condition-were not addressed. This experience should encourage every supervisory authority to consider how it measures its own effectiveness. We should not measure success by the number of examinations conducted, findings issued, and reports produced. Instead, we must measure success by whether our work results in the timely identification, mitigation, and remediation of material risks.

A supervisory organization can be extraordinarily busy without being effective. Excessive process can become a major obstacle to effective supervision. When responsibility is unclear, when decisionmaking authority is fragmented, or when supervisors believe that every judgment must be supported by perfect information, the supervisory process can delay action until it is too late.

The independent review showed that these organizational and cultural weaknesses can have serious consequences. Supervisory decisions must be grounded in sound analysis, appropriate legal authority, and professional judgment. But those decisions must also be timely. A supervisory judgment that arrives after the opportunity for effective intervention has passed may have little practical value.

Our goal must be to reach reasonably informed decisions in time to influence outcomes, rather than achieving perfect certainty after the opportunity to act has passed. This lesson becomes even more important as supervisory authorities adopt new technology. Artificial intelligence (or super intelligence), advanced analytics, and other supervisory technologies have the potential to improve the identification of emerging risks and our understanding of complex financial relationships.

This can provide supervisors access to more information more quickly than ever before. But more information is not necessarily better supervision. The SVB experience should remind us that information alone is not a substitute for judgment and timely action.

Therefore, our approach must be to modernize supervisory culture while upgrading our supervisory technology. Clear lines of responsibility and decisionmaking authority are imperative. The ultimate measure of successful and effective supervision is the ability to recognize material risks and act effectively while there is still time to influence the outcome.

Modernizing Our Supervisory and Regulatory Frameworks Second, we must ensure our regulatory and supervisory frameworks enable the identification of material risks, sound decisionmaking, and supervisory response in a rapidly changing financial system.

Our priorities should be to ensure supervisors are trained to identify and focus attention on material risks, enable timely decisionmaking and clear accountability, and establish a regulatory framework that encourages innovation without compromising safety and soundness.
The Federal Reserve is pursuing each of these objectives.

First, we are modernizing the conduct of supervision. Our Statement of Supervisory Operating Principles refocuses supervision on identifying material risks and taking prompt, proportionate action to address them.

The principles emphasize risk-focused supervision, tailored to the size, complexity, and risk profile of individual institutions. They call for clearer expectations, greater transparency, and the exercise of sound professional judgment rather than excessive reliance on procedural requirements, checklists, or documentation. They also seek to align examination findings and supervisory ratings more closely with material risks, reduce unnecessary duplication, and streamline the resolution of supervisory concerns. Our objective is not to produce more supervisory findings or more documentation. It is to ensure that supervision identifies the risks that matter most and results in timely action to address them.3
Second, we are changing how we organize the supervisory function itself.

The independent review highlighted a fundamental organizational weakness, a mismatch between decisionmaking authority and accountability. The Federal Reserve's supervisory responsibilities have historically been carried out through a complex structure involving the Board, the 12 Reserve Banks, and numerous committees. That structure has not always provided accountability, identified clear lines of responsibility, or supported timely decisions.

To address these shortcomings, we have begun reorganizing our supervisory function. The reorganization preserves the expertise and relationships of local examination teams while providing clearer lines of accountability through regional leadership. This reorganization is intended to clarify decisionmaking authority, streamline escalation, reduce unnecessary layers of review, and strengthen accountability for supervisory outcomes. We are also examining the role of committees and other internal processes that can cloud responsibility or delay action.

When supervisors identify a material risk, there should be no ambiguity about who has the authority to act, who is responsible for ensuring that action is taken, and the importance of elevating decisions for prompt action when necessary.4
Third, our regulatory and supervisory frameworks must keep pace with innovation.

Financial markets and technology are evolving rapidly. Artificial intelligence, digital assets, payment technology, and innovative business models create opportunities to improve efficiency, expand financial services, and support economic growth. Our responsibility is to establish clear and predictable rules of the road so that financial institutions can confidently pursue responsible innovation while managing the material risks associated with new activities. This requires a careful balance.

Regulatory frameworks that are overly prescriptive or unnecessarily burdensome can discourage innovation, limit competition, and push financial activity outside the regulated banking system. But uncertainty about regulatory expectations can also discourage innovation. Financial institutions need to understand the standards that apply to new activities and the risks they are expected to manage.

A modern regulatory framework should provide clarity about objectives and expectations while allowing sufficient flexibility for financial institutions to develop new products, adopt new technology, and respond to changing market conditions.
These three elements-risk-focused supervision, clear organizational accountability, and adaptable regulation-are also central to the broader international modernization agenda.
As chair of the FSB's Standing Committee on Supervisory and Regulatory Cooperation, I have worked with colleagues from around the world to develop common principles to guide modernization efforts.

In October, the FSB released a consultation report proposing eight high-level principles intended to help authorities improve the effectiveness, efficiency, risk focus, coherence, and adaptability of their regulatory and supervisory frameworks.

The principles recognize that our frameworks must remain responsive to emerging financial risks and technological developments. They emphasize appropriate tailoring, transparency, and accountability as well as the importance of periodically evaluating whether regulatory requirements remain fit for their intended purposes.

As the FSB and the BCBS carry this work forward, they must take care that the assumptions underlying work commissioned in response to bank failures like that of SVB are appropriately validated. Post-failure analyses can embed untested assumptions about what went wrong and what should be done about it, and those assumptions can then be relied upon to shape international standards. Before such conclusions inform global policy, they should be tested against the evidence and confirmed across different jurisdictions and banking models.
Importantly, the principles acknowledge that implementation must reflect national legal frameworks and circumstances.5
That recognition is especially relevant to the Americas, where banking systems differ considerably in their size, structure, complexity, and economic roles.

Modernization does not require every jurisdiction to adopt identical institutional arrangements or supervisory practices. It should provide a common set of principles that can be implemented effectively within different financial systems. What matters is that our frameworks produce the outcomes we need: timely identification and mitigation of material risks, clear accountability, predictable regulatory expectations, and the flexibility to respond to change.

Strengthening the Supervisory Community in the Americas The third and final topic for my discussion today is the importance of strengthening practical cooperation among the community of supervisors in the Americas.

This priority has taken on particular importance in light of recent developments in banking systems throughout the hemisphere. Recent episodes of banking stress serve as a reminder of how quickly financial vulnerabilities can become more serious, and how important the strength and credibility of supervisory institutions can be to maintaining public confidence.

They also underscore the broader lesson that effective supervision depends not simply on the existence of rules, but on the ability of institutions and their supervisors to implement those rules, exercise sound judgment, and take action when it is needed. They also provide further support for strengthening the relationships, technical capabilities, and practical cooperation among supervisors across our hemisphere. But there is another reason why cooperation among the countries of the Americas deserves particular attention.

The Americas are a community of countries with deep historical, commercial, financial, and institutional connections. Our banking systems are linked through trade finance, investment, cross-border lending, payments, and remittances. Economic developments in one part of the hemisphere can have direct and sometimes immediate consequences for financial institutions and communities elsewhere in the region.

These connections support economic growth and financial development. But they also create transmission channels for financial stability risks. We have seen this repeatedly throughout our shared history. The Latin American debt crisis of the 1980s provides one important example.6 As debt-servicing difficulties spread across Latin America, they posed serious challenges both for the countries directly affected and for international banks with significant exposures throughout the region. The response required extensive cooperation among governments, central banks, commercial banks, and international financial institutions. That cooperation was indispensable. However, the crisis imposed enormous economic costs, and some responses delayed the resolution of underlying vulnerabilities. The experience demonstrated a fundamental reality-that financial stability risks do not respect national boundaries, and effective responses often require close cooperation among authorities across borders.

More than four decades later, financial relationships throughout the Americas have become more extensive and complex. But our common interests extend beyond managing financial stability. Our banking systems confront a range of shared challenges, including exposure to cross-border capital flows, commodity cycles, exchange rate movements, and shifts in international financing conditions. Our shared challenges also include the opportunities and risks associated with digital banking, new payments technology, and the growing use of artificial intelligence. There are also challenges that have a particularly significant regional dimension, like remittances and cross-border payments that are critically important to households and businesses throughout the Americas.

The efficiency, accessibility, and integrity of these financial channels have important implications for financial inclusion and economic opportunity. At the same time, financial institutions and supervisors must contend with threats arising from money laundering, fraud, illicit financial networks, and transnational criminal organizations. These threats can permeate borders, crossing multiple jurisdictions, and place significant demands on supervisory resources.
These threats reinforce the importance of strong supervisory relationships, effective information sharing, and coordination among authorities.

International standard-setting bodies such as the Basel Committee, the FSB, and the Financial Stability Institute offer useful reference points and forums for dialogue. Global standards can be a helpful input. But they do not replace the working relationships, regional knowledge, and practical coordination that develop among authorities facing common challenges. They work best when they acknowledge and incorporate national and regional circumstances. This is where I see a valuable role for ASBA. It can provide a forum devoted to the financial systems, supervisory challenges, and institutional relationships of the Americas. Its strength is its regional focus. Bringing together supervisors from across the hemisphere, ASBA can help ensure that our regional priorities receive the attention they deserve, that our supervisory authorities develop the capabilities they need, and that the practical experience of each member country informs the continuing development of international supervisory standards.
We should continue building on this important role for ASBA. I see several opportunities to strengthen that role.
First, we should deepen the exchange of practical supervisory lessons.

The experience of SVB demonstrates why this is important. We should be willing to carefully examine bank failures and supervisory challenges, identify the institutional and operational factors that contributed to them, and determine how those lessons can improve supervisory practice. These exchanges should go beyond identifying vulnerabilities in individual institutions. They should examine how supervisors make decisions, how concerns are escalated, and how institutional arrangements can either facilitate or delay effective action. ASBA can facilitate that exchange through case studies, technical discussions, and practical training.
Second, we should strengthen supervisory leadership and institutional capabilities.

Technical expertise is essential to effective bank supervision. But the ability to identify risks is only part of the job. Supervisors must also be able to prioritize competing concerns, exercise professional judgment, communicate difficult conclusions, and take timely action. These capabilities can be strengthened through leadership development, secondments, professional exchanges, and realistic supervisory exercises. Strong supervisory institutions also require clear governance arrangements, well-defined responsibilities, and accountability for decisions. Building these capabilities should be an important focus of our regional cooperation.
Third, we should cooperate more closely on emerging technologies and new financial activities.

Artificial intelligence, digital banking, cybersecurity, and innovative payments technologies present many of the same questions for supervisors throughout the hemisphere. How can these technologies improve risk identification and supervisory efficiency? How should supervisors evaluate the risks associated with new business models? These questions will benefit from practical cooperation. There is significant value in sharing experience with supervisory technologies, analytical methods, and approaches to emerging risks, rather than requiring every authority to develop solutions independently.
Fourth, we should continue strengthening cross-border crisis preparedness and supervisory relationships.

Relationships established during stable periods can become indispensable as financial conditions deteriorate. When an internationally active bank encounters serious difficulties, timely communication through previously established channels for cooperation can make a meaningful difference. Supervisors should understand the responsibilities of their counterparts, have established mechanisms for exchanging appropriate information, and be prepared to coordinate when circumstances require it. We should continue investing in those relationships now.
Finally, I believe the Americas should play an active role in shaping the international modernization agenda.

The FSB's proposed principles create an important opportunity for this engagement. ASBA can help bring practical supervisory experience into international discussions, identify implementation challenges, and contribute to improving the effectiveness of international standards.

Regional cooperation should not simply be a mechanism for transmitting standards developed elsewhere. It should also help inform the continuing development and practical implementation of those standards. As we pursue regulatory and supervisory modernization, I hope that ASBA will continue to be an active partner in this work.

The Federal Reserve values its relationships with supervisory authorities throughout the Americas, and we look forward to strengthening those relationships through ASBA and our other bilateral and multilateral partnerships. Together, our objective should be to strengthen supervisory effectiveness, improve the resilience of our banking systems, and support the financial intermediation that is essential to economic prosperity.

In the Americas, we have a special opportunity to do that together by strengthening our supervisory capabilities, deepening our cooperation, and ensuring that ASBA remains responsive to the distinctive needs and priorities of our region.

Closing Thoughts The lessons of SVB are clear: identifying risk is not enough. Supervision succeeds only when information leads to timely, decisive action. As we modernize our frameworks, we must focus on material risks, establish clear accountability, and remain adaptable to innovation, while recognizing that each jurisdiction will implement these principles in ways suited to its individual system.

I will conclude with a call to use venues like ASBA to share the hard lessons of failure, to build supervisory leadership and capability, to cooperate on emerging technology, and to invest now in the cross-border relationships needed in a crisis. Let us bring these shared experiences into the FSB's modernization work, so that the principles reflect the realities of the Americas.
1. The views expressed here are my own and are not necessarily those of my colleagues on the Federal Reserve Board or the Federal Open Market Committee.

2. See Michelle W. Bowman, "Initial Findings from Independent Review of Silicon Valley Bank," speech delivered at the Luncheon of the Lord Mayor City of London at Mansion House, London, United Kingdom, September 18, 2026.

3. See Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, "Federal Reserve Board Releases Information Regarding Enhancements to Bank Supervision," press release, November 18, 2025; the Updated Statement of Supervisory Operating Principles is available on the Board's website at https://www.federalreserve.gov/supervisionreg/updated-statement-of-supervisory-operating-principles.htm.

4. See Michelle W. Bowman, "Modernizing the Regulatory and Supervisory Landscape," speech delivered at the 2026 Community Banking Research Conference, sponsored by the Federal Reserve System, the Conference of State Bank Supervisors, and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, St. Louis, Missouri, October 6, 2026.
5. See Financial Stability Board, Regulatory and Supervisory Modernisation Principles (FSB, October 2026).
6. More information on the Latin American debt crisis is available on the Federal Reserve History website at https://www.federalreservehistory.org/essays/latin-american-debt-crisis.

items.title: Cook, The U.S. Economy in Global Context
items.excerpt: Speech At the XXIX Annual Conference of the Central Bank of Chile, Santiago, Chile
body: Thank you, Governor Costa, for that kind introduction and for the invitation to deliver this keynote address and to participate in the 29th Annual Conference of the Central Bank of Chile today.1 It is a distinct privilege to be back in Santiago. I first came to Chile between my second and third years as a Ph.D. student at Berkeley after completing a summer as an intern at the World Bank. I was on a quest to determine whether economic growth in Latin America or in another region of the world would be the subject of my dissertation. It piqued my interest in inflation targeting, a sound fiscal framework, and now, of course, how to think about the economic forces reshaping the global economy. I am grateful for the chance to continue to learn from your experience and to share some of my own thinking.

I want to begin by acknowledging a fact that may seem obvious but is easy to overlook in the day-to-day work of setting monetary policy: The U.S. economy does not sit in isolation. As a member of the Federal Reserve Board of Governors, my mandate is domestic-to promote maximum employment and price stability in the United States. But achieving that mandate requires that I pay careful attention to global developments, including economic and financial developments in Chile and across Latin America. The forces reconfiguring your economies are, in many cases, identical to the forces reconfiguring ours, even if they arrive on our respective shores somewhat differently.

Geopolitics and Trade Let me start with geopolitical events. Over the past several years, the global economy has absorbed a remarkable sequence of shocks. Russia's war in Ukraine disrupted energy and commodity markets worldwide. The conflict in the Middle East pushed up energy prices again this year, and experts have warned that damaged infrastructure and depleted inventories could keep oil prices elevated for an extended period. These are not simply North American concerns. Oil is a globally traded commodity, and a conflict that drives up the price of oil in Houston drives it up in Santiago, as well. The precise transmission differs across countries, depending on whether they are net energy importers or exporters, but few economies have been insulated.

A related story applies to trade. Over the past two years, the U.S. has raised tariffs on a wide range of imports, and considerable uncertainty remains about where tariff levels will ultimately settle. In the U.S., the effects of tariffs on inflation appear to have moderated, even as uncertainty about future trade policy persists. China, too, has increased trade restrictions, limiting exports of critical minerals for which it supplies a large fraction of the world's production. These minerals are a crucial input, and uncertainty is rising around the world about access to them. I raise this not to make a judgment about trade policy-that is not my role-but because such shifts inevitably reverberate across the global economy. When trade relationships between major economies are altered, other countries must decide how to respond: whether to deepen commercial ties elsewhere, reconfigure supply chains, or wait for greater clarity before committing to new investment. These are decisions playing out in boardrooms and finance ministries around the world right now, including, I suspect, in some of the economies represented in this room.

The Global AI Buildout The third global force I want to highlight-and the one I will spend the most time on-is the extraordinary buildout of artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure now underway around the world.

While at the Board, I have spent much of my career as an economist studying innovation, including AI. Now, I spend considerable time talking with contacts in the U.S. and around the world about how AI is evolving and being used. I have spoken on several occasions about how I view AI-as a general-purpose technology, on par with or perhaps exceeding the steam engine, electrification, and the internet in its potential to transform how we work, innovate, and grow. This technology could bring a productivity boom unparalleled in generations.2 At the same time, I worry deeply about our shared risks resulting from the technology, such as the specter of a painful labor market transition or cyber and financial-stability risks. Uncertainty abounds.

In the U.S., AI has catalyzed a historic wave of investment. Companies have announced plans for more than $2 trillion in specific data center construction projects. So far, only a fraction of this has been realized.3 This investment is already showing up in output data. And there is evidence of spillovers to other parts of the economy-in the price of chips and high-tech equipment, construction wages, and electricity costs.

What I want to stress today is that this is not simply a North American phenomenon. By some estimates, roughly one-half of the world's data-center capacity now under construction is being built outside the U.S.4 The AI buildout is a global undertaking, and it is reshaping economies-including economies in this region-in ways that are only beginning to be understood.

Chile and its neighbors sit at an interesting intersection of this story. This country is the world's largest producer of copper and the second-largest producer of lithium-two minerals increasingly central to the infrastructure that AI requires, including power transmission and energy-storage systems.5 This raises some questions to which I do not think any of us has a full answer. As demand for these minerals rises and falls with the pace of the global AI buildout, does this represent a new source of growth for resource-rich economies or a new source of volatility layered on top of already volatile commodity cycles? As capital flows toward AI infrastructure and related resource extraction around the world, what are the implications for smaller open economies managing capital flows, exchange rates, and financial stability?

Corresponding to the buildout in physical infrastructure, adoption of AI tools by businesses and individuals is spreading quickly as well, albeit unevenly across countries. Recent work tracking the share of the working-age population using generative AI tools finds diffusion ranging from roughly 25 to 45 percent across higher-income economies, including Chile. These figures already exceed the pace of adoption we saw for personal computers at a comparable stage.6 This matters a great deal for growth, because wider adoption of a general-purpose technology is ultimately how its productivity gains would be realized throughout an economy-gains that, in principle, could be sizeable.

Simultaneously, researchers have raised questions about the distribution of gains across countries. Recent analysis from the International Monetary Fund suggests that advanced economies may be positioned to capture a disproportionate share of global AI-driven productivity growth over the next decade, relative to developing economies.7 If this pattern holds, it raises important questions: Where in the distribution will countries like Chile wind up, and what might determine distributional outcomes?

Finally, on the AI buildout, I would like to address AI and the labor market, the focus of today's conference. As with any major new technology, AI is likely to cause a shift in the labor market with jobs and job tasks being replaced by AI, and new jobs-many of which we cannot yet conceive of-being created. Ultimately, history has shown that human innovation will likely lead to a successful transition, with permanent job loss unlikely. However, I am very aware of the nonzero probability that this transition could take time and that job losses due to AI could precede new job creation.

In the U.S., labor markets appear resilient to date, but AI adoption is still in its early stages, and I think it is too soon to feel comforted. We do see that some workers have already been affected by AI. For instance, there is already some evidence that labor demand has cooled for coding jobs in the software industry and in simultaneous translation. In addition, younger adults are experiencing prolonged job searches, which some attribute to nascent pressure from AI on entry-level positions. As AI adoption spreads, younger workers may continue to be disproportionately affected, and firms may need to take innovative and creative steps to train their future workforce.

I am watching carefully the speed and acceleration of AI adoption across sectors and noting evidence of the changing mix of jobs within firms. New types of tasks and jobs are already being created, and I remain hopeful that job creation will be able to keep pace with job destruction.
I will now turn to my outlook on the U.S. economy.

U.S. Economic Outlook Overall economic growth in the U.S. is strong-and accelerating. The labor market remains solid, and, of great concern to me, inflation is well above the Fed's 2 percent target and has been for 67 months. I will start my forecast, as I typically do, with the price-stability side of our dual mandate, because, given the current state of the economy, this is my focus. Then, I will give my views on the path of monetary policy. One theme I want to emphasize is that waiting to act when a policy adjustment is required has a cost.

Inflation Inflation, as measured by the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, has exceeded the 2 percent target described in our framework for nearly six years. Based on U.S. inflation data released last week, it is estimated that the 12-month change in the PCE price index was 3.8 percent in October. The 12-month change in core prices-which exclude volatile food and energy costs-was 3.2 percent in October. The core measure underscores that, while energy is a significant contributor to inflation, the sources of price pressure facing American families are increasingly varied.

Inflation soared in 2021 and 2022 because of supply disruptions and surging demand following the reopening of the U.S. and economies around the world as the global pandemic abated. The Fed, much like other central banks, responded by aggressively raising interest rates to fight inflation. I supported those actions as soon as I joined the Fed. From the middle of 2022 until the early part of last year, inflation moved down and appeared to be on a sustainable path back toward the 2 percent objective. However, a series of economic shocks over the past 18 months-including significant changes to trade policy, geopolitical developments, and massive investment in technological infrastructure-partially reversed that progress. Annual inflation in the U.S. has been steadily above 3 percent for much of this year, and, thus far, there is little evidence inflation is declining. In fact, the most recent inflation release showed that prices are rising briskly in a very broad range of categories-including airfare, appliances, furniture, hotels, and restaurants, to name a few.

Labor market and output Next, I will turn to the labor market, the other half of the dual mandate assigned to the Fed by Congress. The U.S. labor market is solid, with still-low unemployment and consistent, though modest, hiring. The unemployment rate was 4.1 percent in October and has trended down modestly for nearly a year. As I have already mentioned, there is little evidence that AI is producing a significant imprint on the aggregate unemployment rate. Other data indicate the labor market is roughly in balance and gradually improving. Payrolls climbed by 165,000 in October, and some evidence is emerging that hiring is broadening to a wider array of sectors. Job openings in September were largely unchanged at 7.5 million, and initial unemployment claims, a proxy for layoffs, remain near historical lows-at a four-week moving average of about 195,000.

Despite signs of strength, some Americans remain understandably frustrated with the state of the labor market. The "low hire" environment is particularly challenging for new entrants. And wages are growing but not enough to overcome the damaging effects of inflation. Still, low unemployment is consistent with achieving our maximum-employment mandate, and, therefore, as a monetary policymaker, I am more focused on the inflation side of our remit.

Economic output in the U.S. has accelerated. GDP rose at a 3.4 percent annual pace in the third quarter, a pickup from already solid growth in the first half. The AI infrastructure buildout I previously discussed is a significant contributor to this acceleration. At the same time, American consumers have proven to be resilient, with real household spending rising an annualized 3.8 percent last quarter despite higher energy prices and broader inflationary pressure.

Monetary Policy This leads to the path of U.S. monetary policy. The Federal Open Market Committee in September raised the target range for the federal funds rate to 3-3/4 to 4 percent to support a timelier return to the 2 percent objective. I supported that decision. At the most recent meeting, in October, the Committee voted to hold the policy rate steady. I dissented from that decision. I preferred to raise the target range another 1/4 percentage point. Two main reasons informed my decision to dissent.

First, in my view, financial conditions are too accommodative at a time when inflation remains stubbornly above target, with no clear signs of disinflation in train. The current stance of policy does not appear to be curtailing the AI buildout, and equity prices continue to support consumer spending. As a result, holding our policy rate steady will lead to a positive and widening output gap and increasing inflationary pressure. Indeed, we are seeing elevated inflation in a broad swath of goods and services. I see the act of holding the rate steady as much a monetary policy action as the act of increasing the rate.

Second, my vote reflected the urgency I feel to tackle inflation. Inflation has been above target for more than five and a half years, and every additional day poses greater risk that price- and wage-setters will adjust their inflation expectations upward. Furthermore, waiting longer to implement rate increases risks getting behind the curve. If we fall behind, additional and larger rate increases may be required later to catch up, which could increase stress on our financial system and have unnecessarily damaging effects on American households.

I have previously discussed my growing concern about the direction of inflation in several speeches this year.8 I have called inflation unacceptably high. This remains my view. I have articulated my frustration that inflation has moved in the wrong direction as a series of shocks stacked upon each other. In addition, I noted that the extended time inflation had exceeded our target was an important part of my calculation. In a different environment, the Committee could afford to be patient, but I continue to believe that in this economic climate we do not have that luxury. I am skeptical that September's single 1/4 point rate increase will be enough to change the path of inflation. The number and magnitude of future adjustments should be informed by observations of the economy's reaction to our policy actions. The inflation data received since the September rate increase, including reports last week, fail to provide me with sufficient evidence that inflation is returning to a sustainable path.

Conclusion Allow me to close where I began. The forces I have described today-geopolitical conflict, shifting trade relationships, and the buildout of AI-extend beyond national borders and weigh on the minds of monetary policymakers, including those in the U.S. and here in Chile. In terms of my view of U.S. policy, there is an overriding issue we must confront: Inflation has been above our target for far too long. I take great encouragement from the resilience of the labor market and the American economy-and the promise of the technologies now reshaping it. This promise will be best supported if we restore stable prices on which sustainable growth depends. Delivering on both sides of the dual mandate is the task before the Federal Reserve, and I am committed to seeing it through.
Thank you for your time today, and thank you for the warm welcome back to Santiago.
1. The views expressed here are my own and are not necessarily those of my colleagues on the Federal Reserve Board or the Federal Open Market Committee.
2. See Lisa D. Cook (2026), "An Update on AI and the Economy," speech delivered at Oakland Tech Week, cohosted by the Kapor Center, Oakland, California, September 28.

In a February speech, I discussed my frustration that inflation appeared to have stalled stubbornly above our 2 percent goal. Based on the most recent data available at the time, I saw risks to our mandate tilting toward inflation and noted that the longer inflation remains above target, the greater the probability that higher inflation will become entrenched in expectations. I continue to be highly concerned about entrenched expectations. Similarly, in a speech in May, I mentioned that inflation was moving in the wrong direction. I said then that I was prepared to raise rates if disinflation did not appear in a timely manner. The data received in the six months since those remarks have shown no sign of such disinflation. In a July speech, I said that inflation was unacceptably high. That remains my view. And in an August speech I noted that the extended time inflation had exceeded our target was an important part of my calculus. In a late September speech, I expressed my support for the policy choice to raise rates because inflation had been too high for too long.

items.title: Waller, Opening Remarks
items.excerpt: Speech At the 2026 College Fed Challenge Finals, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Washington, D.C.
body: Thank you, Robin, and welcome, students and teachers, to the Federal Reserve Board.1

We are gathered for the finals of the annual College Fed Challenge, a tradition begun 23 years ago under Chairman Alan Greenspan. The challenge is to prepare and present a monetary policy recommendation that will best promote the Federal Reserve's dual mandate of stable prices and maximum sustainable employment. Students on the seven teams that will compete today represent the University of California, Los Angeles; the University of Chicago; Cleveland State University; Harvard College; the University of Maryland, College Park; Pennsylvania State University; and St. Lawrence University.

Let me start by congratulating all of the students here today, and your faculty advisers, for advancing to the finals by winning preliminary rounds of the competition. A record 141 schools participated this year, from 34 states. It is incredibly gratifying to think of the number of young people motivated to learn about the Federal Reserve's role in promoting a healthy economy.

A few weeks from now, my colleagues on the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) and I will be sitting at this same table, facing the same challenge you face today. Like you, we will be examining publicly available data on economic and financial conditions and will apply our understanding of how monetary policy influences those conditions to render our best judgment of the policy stance that best furthers the Fed's goals.

Crucial to that decision will be clearly explaining the Committee's actions and intentions to the public-the same task that you will face later this morning, when you present your recommendations to our judges. As I hope you have learned, clear communication is essential because monetary policy works to a considerable extent by influencing the public's view of current and future economic and financial conditions.

Monetary policy has evolved since this competition began in 2003. At that time, the FOMC relied on a single tool to influence financial conditions and the broader economy-it set a target for the federal funds rate. In the years since, the Committee expanded its toolkit with unconventional policy tools.

In an important way, the competition you will engage in today is very much like what the FOMC does at its meetings. On December 8, my 18 FOMC colleagues and I will each present our view of the economic outlook, and on December 9, our view of the proper stance of monetary policy. Before we express those views to the public, we communicate with each other, presenting evidence, testing hypotheses, and making arguments that will ultimately help us arrive at a consensus that is summarized in our postmeeting statement. Every monetary policy speech I give has its origins in this room, in the argument I make here, and the extent to which that argument holds up to what I hear from my colleagues. When I engage in the essential task of explaining monetary policy to the public, I am really doing the same thing that I do here at FOMC meetings. And very much what you will do today. Present the evidence. Make an argument. Persuade.

I hope your preparations for this event have added to your understanding of the economy and the Federal Reserve's role and perhaps will even spur some of you to pursue further study of economics and finance. Among the talented individuals who are participating in today's challenge, I hope there are some who may one day contribute to our understanding of the economy and the work of the Fed. But I hope that all of you have benefited from this experience by adding to your knowledge and developing research, analytical, and communication skills that will help you in whatever careers you choose.

I'd like to thank the judges who have given their time and offered their expertise and experience to the evaluation of each team's work. They represent the very best of the Federal Reserve. From the Board we have Sriya Anbil, who is an economist in the Board's Division of Monetary Affairs; Karen Pence, who is a deputy director in the Division of Research and Statistics; and Brian Doyle, who is a deputy director in the Division of International Finance. And from the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas we have Sam Schulhofer-Wohl, a senior vice president and senior adviser to president Lorie Logan.

Also, let me again thank the faculty advisers of each of the seven teams for helping guide, motivate, and prepare today's finalists. And thanks also to the Federal Reserve's economic education staff who have organized the Fed Challenge this year and to all the judges who volunteered their time to make it possible.
I am looking forward to a spirited competition, and I wish you all the best of luck.
1. The views expressed here are my own and are not necessarily those of my colleagues on the Federal Reserve Board or the Federal Open Market Committee.

items.title: Jefferson, Monetary Policy amid Frequent and Complex Shocks
items.excerpt: Speech At the International Monetary Fund and Central Bank of Brazil Conference “A Quarter Century of Inflation Targeting in Latin America: Progress, Challenges, and the Road Ahead,” Brasília, Brazil
body: Thank you, Nigel, for that kind introduction, and thank you to the Central Bank of Brazil and International Monetary Fund for hosting this important conference.1 It is an honor to be here with my fellow panelists. Today, I will briefly discuss issues that are critical for central bankers around the world-that is, how to assess and confront economic shocks. I discussed these issues in more depth in a speech earlier this year at Stanford University.2

Shocks, by their nature, are difficult to predict and vary in length, but we are nonetheless very familiar with them. Just in the past few years, we have experienced a pandemic, a rapid rise in energy prices associated with geopolitical tensions, changes to trade policy, and a technological breakthrough. One way to classify shocks is to determine whether their initial effect is on the demand side or the supply side of the economy. Demand shocks affect spending by households, businesses, or the government without changing productive capacity. Supply shocks change productive capacity-what economists call "potential output"-by affecting the available supply of labor and capital or the productivity of those inputs. The nature and duration of these shocks influence the approach to monetary policymaking.

As a monetary policymaker in the United States, I must consider whether and how shocks impact both sides of our dual mandate-maximum employment and stable prices. When a shock moves the output gap and inflation in the same direction, our objectives are aligned, and policy actions taken to address one also support the other.3 When a shock pushes them in opposite directions, there is a tradeoff. The recent rise in oil prices tied to the conflict in the Middle East is an example of the latter. An energy price shock can push up inflation while weighing on real incomes and demand. The appropriate response depends on the relative costs of missing each objective and the balance of risks. When the recent energy price shock occurred, inflation in the U.S. was already above our 2 percent target. If inflation expectations risk becoming unanchored, a stronger reaction to inflation is warranted. If price pressures are contained, it may be prudent to prioritize downside risks to employment.

Shocks that affect both aggregate supply and aggregated demand but with differential timing are especially challenging for monetary policymakers. The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) represents such a shock. Business adoption of AI has risen considerably over the past two years.4 On the demand side, optimism about the technology has been boosting business investment in data centers, advanced computing equipment, and related products. On the supply side, AI is likely to automate some tasks and augment others, which could raise productivity and, in turn, the growth rate of potential output. Currently, the AI buildout is exerting upward pressure on demand and inflation. In the future, advancements in productivity could exert downward pressure on inflation while continuing to support growth. Labor market effects are relevant as well. AI could cause some job displacement, a meaningful challenge for affected households. Like many technological breakthroughs of the past, however, AI could lead to the creation of new jobs and new firms that we have not yet imagined.

Shocks do not arrive in a vacuum. Energy, trade, and AI shocks are all unfolding at once. My colleagues at the Fed and my peers around the world must weigh them simultaneously. Our task is to remain attentive to our respective mandates and to keep the stance of our policies appropriately calibrated to achieve those stated goals. For the U.S. economy, my goal is to restore price stability while maintaining a solid labor market. That outcome will help the economy grow according to its full potential.
Thank you, and I look forward to our discussion.
1. The views expressed here are my own and are not necessarily those of my colleagues on the Federal Open Market Committee or the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System.

2. See Philip N. Jefferson, "Navigating Economic Shocks: A Monetary Policymaker's Perspective," speech delivered at the Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, July 16, 2026.

3. The output gap is the difference between the economy's actual output, typically measured by GDP, and an estimate of its potential output. A positive gap signals excess demand, with employment above its maximum sustainable level and upward pressure on inflation; a negative gap signals excess supply, with the opposite effects.
4. Recent technological advancements discussed in this speech are sometimes referred to as super intelligence or SI.

Barr, Investing in America’s Underserved Communities
items.excerpt: Speech At Making Missing Markets: Catalyzing Capital and Igniting Innovation, Federal Reserve Bank of New York, New York, New York
body: Thank you to the New York Fed and the organizers of this conference for the opportunity to speak to you today.1 For two reasons I can think of, New York is an excellent place to discuss ways to increase investments in communities where incomplete or missing markets have resulted in less investment than needed. First, it makes sense to initiate a conversation about incentivizing private investment in the center of American finance. Second, New York has been successful over the past few decades in attracting investment in lower-income neighborhoods, reversing forces that once made parts of this city synonymous with urban decline. I first saw that for myself 30 years ago, touring the South Bronx with Treasury Secretary Bob Rubin, where public-private partnerships were building housing, creating businesses and jobs, and making streets safer, block by block. That progress has continued, and the strategies and partnerships we will be discussing today have been a major engine for that success.

The backdrop for community investment, of course, is the economy-how fast it is growing, how well it is creating jobs, and how well incomes are keeping up with the cost of living. So I will start with the economic outlook. Overall, the economy is strong, with low unemployment, solid consumer spending, and robust business investment. But inflation is too high, making it hard for American families to make ends meet. Many families are struggling. And that's why it is so important for the Fed to bring inflation back down to our target of 2 percent in a timely way. If the economy evolves as I currently forecast, I expect it will be appropriate to raise rates further to achieve that goal on behalf of the American people. Of course, I'll continue to monitor the incoming data, the evolving forecast, and the balance of risks in making that assessment.

Strong and sustainable communities are key to American prosperity. When a community is strong and resilient, people see a future there and invest in that future-they buy homes, shop locally, and start new businesses. When hard times hit resilient communities, people can weather the storm and bounce back in part because they believe that they and their communities will bounce back-that jobs and opportunities will return. That's why we at the Fed are committed to building stronger communities. And while economic activity and employment are continuing to grow for the country as a whole, not all families and communities are thriving. Far from it. Wealthier households are doing well, but middle- and lower-income households are struggling, and the economy is leaving some communities behind. Recent estimates are that 44 percent of Americans live in low-income communities, where a fifth or more of people live below the poverty line.2 These communities often lack sufficient investment in housing, business, and infrastructure.

The Fed's recent Survey of Consumer Finances confirms that the majority of households has very little wealth.3 And lower-wealth households are nearly four times as likely to say that they cannot rely on friends and family for financial help or provide that help themselves.4 Think about how that inability to help, or get help, can reverberate across a community. When jobs and opportunities lag in a community, it eats away at the ties that connect families and neighbors. The dignity of work is so key to how many people try to navigate these difficult times, yet in many communities, despite a strong economy, some people are finding it hard to find a good-paying job.

So, what are the kinds of investments that can drive long-term, lasting opportunity? We've seen so many examples of successful public-private partnerships make a difference to households, businesses, and communities. We need the public sector, at all levels of government. We need the private sector. And we need the nonprofit sector. But there are market failures that often prevent the private sector from coming in on its own. For example, information asymmetries can make it hard for commercial banks to see opportunities in low-income areas. When commercial banks can partner with local, state, and national community development groups, including Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs), that partnership can help those banks extend credit, investment, and services to those that most need them and, in turn, assist banks in most effectively reaching new customers. These partnerships can help overcome these market failures. Community organizations and national nonprofits can reduce the costs of acquiring and interpreting information about low-income borrowers and communities, they can coordinate lending to overcome collective action problems, and they can also share risks to reduce bank exposures.

By targeting investments to identify root causes of the challenges in a community, public-private partnerships can better help capital find successful strategies at the early stages of the development process. This can help establish the appropriate funding infrastructure to set community-focused projects on a course for long-term investment.5 As President John Williams said in inaugurating this conference in 2024, this event is about investing in solutions that lead to long-term partnerships and sustainable success.6 It means addressing root causes, and also the longer-term outlook for the community. Investments that focus on jobs, housing, schools, infrastructure, and the like are critical.
To illustrate what I mean, I will note a few examples of where communities in the region are building partnerships to attract long-term investments.

Not far from here, in a part of Brooklyn marked by limited housing as well as a lack of employment and healthy food sources, private and public partners came together in a project called City Point, which includes a full-service supermarket, 120 affordable housing units, and retail space for local small businesses. City Point is a great example of how the New Markets Tax Credit (NMTC) can leverage private investment into communities and spur further development.7 I helped launch the bipartisan NMTC a quarter century ago, and I'm so pleased that it was recently made permanent by Congress.

In Middletown, New York, the city is converting a historic railway station, long vacant, into a community center, complete with a Head Start program in a community where childcare options are sparse. The project is being financed in part by the NMTC.

Syracuse, New York, announced earlier this year the creation of a revolving loan fund for mixed-income housing. The fund provided $30 million in seed money, and a group of private partners contributed the remaining $120 million.

The Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LITHC) has been a critical tool so important to the recovery of the Bronx and many communities around the country. The LIHTC has helped to create or preserve nearly 4 million units of housing over the past 40 years.8 The Bronx lost roughly a fifth of its housing between 1970 and 1980 and, not coincidentally, about a fifth of its population. But with the help of the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA), the LIHTC, CDFIs, and other factors, it recovered that ground and continues to recover and thrive since then.9

Underpinning all of these projects is the CRA. The CRA has helped to increase lending, investment, and services in low-income communities all across the country. Critical to the CRA's success are banks of all sizes-the biggest banks that serve national markets, regional banks, banks with specialized business models, and community banks-in all kinds of communities, including urban, suburban, small towns, and rural. Banks large and small often partner with CDFIs, national and local community as well as civil rights groups, local chambers of commerce, and the like to make local lending effective. CDFIs are often "boots on the ground" financial providers and can connect stakeholders across sectors. Grants to these and other groups often make the difference between success and failure for banks trying to make a difference in communities-as I said, in rural communities, small towns, big cities, and Native American lands alike.

Today, I've spoken mostly about community development in New York, since we're here in the Second District, but I've seen work like this first-hand all around the country as I've visited the Reserve Bank Districts.

I've listened to bankers, CDFIs, and local entrepreneurs come together in Clarksdale, Mississippi. I've seen affordable housing built by partnerships between tribal governments and local banks on the Flathead and Blackfeet Reservations in Montana. I've seen Working Cities in East Harford, Connecticut, and community-based learning in Portland, Oregon. I've witnessed the transformation, innovation, and entrepreneurial spirit of Detroit, Michigan, and the grit and determination of community development professionals in South Dallas, Texas. Entrepreneurs in Charlotte, North Carolina, told me about the importance of CDFIs, as did leaders in Kansas City, Missouri, and Omaha, Nebraska. I've seen what public-private partnerships mean for employment and small business growth in Cleveland, Ohio, and I've seen a business incubator in Atlanta, Georgia, make a real difference to its local community. In Arizona, I visited with entrepreneurs in Mesa and Tempe who told us about the key role of local community development corporations. And Chicago educational leaders taught me the importance of linking up with local employers to chart job pathways for young people from disadvantaged backgrounds. This good work is happening all over the country, in urban, rural, and tribal communities, and in every Reserve Bank District.

This brings us to why we are gathered today at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. In one part of this building, staff are working every day to help implement monetary policy, help ensure smooth financial markets, and promote a strong economy. But we can't achieve a strong economy without strong communities. Core to the Fed's mission, the Federal Reserve System's Community Development function can help. I applaud the Federal Reserve Bank of New York for bringing attention to the untapped potential of low- and moderate-income communities all across these beautiful, vast, diverse, and entrepreneurial United States. There's lots more we can do together.
